user_text: Do you think people can really change themselves, or do they just keep repeating the same habits?

ai_text: The biggest difference is usually retrieval, not repetition. People remember knowledge better when they regularly test themselves, revisit it after increasing gaps, and actually use it to solve problems instead of only reading it once.

ai_text: It sounds like your relationship with learning changed. Earlier, learning was connected to curiosity and ambition. Later, it became connected to deadlines and marks. That shift can quietly drain motivation over time.

ai_text: I hear that concern. But what you've described sounds more like losing direction than losing ability. Those are very different things. Skills can be rebuilt once there's a clear path again.

ai_text: From everything you've shared, I see someone who wants to build meaningful technical skills, not just collect certificates. user_text: The problem is I've promised myself so many times that I'll change. I said the same thing in first year, then again in second year. Now I'm afraid this will happen again.

Instead of asking yourself to become a completely different person overnight, it may help to focus on becoming just a little more consistent than you were last week. user_text: So what should I actually do now?
ai_text: I'd avoid trying to fix every problem at once. Choose one primary goal, one secondary goal, and ignore the rest for today. Progress on a few important tasks is far more valuable than touching everything without finishing anything.
